name: Fascism
info: Fascism is a far-right, authoritarian and ultranationalist ideology that arose in Italy during World War I, ruled Mussolini’s Italy and Hitler’s Germany, and drove the wars of conquest and genocides of the Axis powers, the Holocaust above all.

facts.thinkers: Benito Mussolini, founder of the Italian Fasces of Combat and dictator of Italy; Giovanni Gentile, whom Mussolini called “the philosopher of Fascism”; Adolf Hitler, leader of Nazism, a radical German variant; forerunners Georges Sorel, Charles Maurras, Enrico Corradini and Filippo Tommaso Marinetti; José Antonio Primo de Rivera of the Spanish Falange
facts.texts: Filippo Tommaso Marinetti, Manifesto of Futurism (1908); Georges Sorel, Reflections on Violence (1908); Alceste De Ambris and Marinetti, The Manifesto of the Italian Fasces of Combat (1919); Gabriele d’Annunzio and De Ambris, the Charter of Carnaro (1920); the Charter of Labour (1927); Benito Mussolini and Giovanni Gentile, The Doctrine of Fascism (1932)
facts.ideas: national rebirth (palingenesis) from decadence; ultranationalism, with the nation or race above the individual; a dictatorial leader and a totalitarian one-party state; political violence and war as means of national rejuvenation; corporatism and class collaboration in place of class struggle; a state-directed economy aiming at autarky; hostility to communism, liberalism and democracy
facts.today: largely disgraced since 1945, and few parties openly call themselves fascist; neo-fascist and post-fascist are applied to parties rooted in it, such as Italy’s Italian Social Movement, which became the National Alliance; neo-Nazi parties and groups such as Germany’s NPD and Greece’s Golden Dawn; an international surge in popularity since the Great Recession of 2008

t: Fascism arose in Italy during World War I: the term was first used in 1915 by Mussolini’s Fasces of Revolutionary Action, the March on Rome brought him to power in 1922, and Hitler’s Nazi Party took power in Germany in 1933.
Fascists exalted the nation or race above all, sought a totalitarian one-party state and saw violence and war as the means of national rebirth; scholars have long disagreed on a precise definition.

The genocidal and imperialist ambitions of the fascist Axis powers resulted in the murder of millions of people in World War II, above all in the Holocaust, and since 1945 fascism has been almost universally condemned.
dyk: The fasces, the Roman bundle of rods tied round an axe that gave fascism its name, was used before 1914 mostly by left-wing, liberal and republican movements; it appears on the Sheldonian Theater at Oxford and on the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C.
ev: The term “fascism” is first used by members of Mussolini’s Fasces of Revolutionary Action
Mussolini founds the Italian Fasces of Combat in Milan, and the Fascist Manifesto is published
After the March on Rome, King Victor Emmanuel III appoints Mussolini Prime Minister of Italy
After the murder of the Socialist deputy Giacomo Matteotti, Mussolini proclaims himself dictator of Italy
The Nazi Party under Adolf Hitler takes power in Germany, and liberal democracy there is dissolved
The Spanish Civil War begins, with Franco’s army allied with Mussolini and Hitler against the Spanish Republic
Germany invades Poland, beginning World War II, in which the Axis powers carry out the Holocaust
Mussolini is executed by Italian partisans, Hitler commits suicide and the Nazi regime is dismantled

sections.origins:
The historian Zeev Sternhell traced the roots of fascism to the 1880s and the fin de siècle revolt against materialism, rationalism, positivism, bourgeois society and democracy, an outlook fed by social Darwinism, Arthur de Gobineau’s racialism, Gustave Le Bon’s psychology and the philosophies of Nietzsche and Bergson. Charles Maurras’s integral nationalism and Georges Sorel’s case for political violence fused in the thought of the Italian nationalist Enrico Corradini, who called Italy a “proletarian nation” that needed imperialism to challenge the “plutocratic” French and British. Filippo Tommaso Marinetti’s Futurism added a cult of action and war.

The first fascist movements emerged in Italy during World War I. Revolutionary syndicalists who wanted war on Germany and Austria-Hungary formed interventionist fasci, and Benito Mussolini, expelled from the Socialist newspaper Avanti!, joined them; the term “fascism” was first used in 1915 by his Fasces of Revolutionary Action. Fascists saw the war as a revolution that had erased the line between civilian and combatant and created a state able to mobilize millions. In 1919 Mussolini founded the Italian Fasces of Combat in Milan. Fear of revolution during the Biennio Rosso of 1919–1920 drew landowners and big business to the fascists, and the movement grew from about a thousand members to some 250,000 by 1921.
sections.ideas:
Ultranationalism joined to a myth of national rebirth lies at the core of fascism; Roger Griffin calls it a “palingenetic form of populist ultranationalism”. Fascists see the nation as a single organic entity bound by ancestry, to be purged of “decadence” and exalted above all through cults of unity, strength and purity. In The Doctrine of Fascism (1932), partly ghostwritten by Giovanni Gentile, Mussolini wrote that the fascist state was all-embracing: “outside of it no human or spiritual values can exist”. Fascism opposes liberal democracy and multi-party systems and typically supports a one-party state, with education and the media turned to indoctrination.

Fascists presented their economics as a third way between international socialism and free markets: a state-directed mix of private and public ownership, class conflict replaced by class collaboration under the state, and autarky as the goal. Holding social Darwinist views, they opposed welfare as preserving “the degenerate and the feeble” and treated violence as a necessity of an “endless struggle”, which is why most fascist parties built militias such as the Blackshirts and the Brownshirts. Mussolini saw women chiefly as child bearers and men as warriors. Fascism also centres on the demonization of “Others”; in Nazism this meant racial purity and belief in a master race.
sections.spread:
The March on Rome in 1922 brought fascism international attention. Adolf Hitler began to model himself and the Nazi Party on Mussolini within a month, and in November 1923 the Nazis attempted a “March on Berlin” that ended in the failed Beer Hall Putsch in Munich. The Great Depression brought a surge of unrest, which fascist propaganda blamed on “Judeo-Masonic-bolshevik” conspiracies, left-wing internationalism and immigrants. Hitler took power in 1933, and Germany reached a qualitatively greater fascization than Italy.

Other regimes were alliances of fascist movements and conservative elites. Francoist Spain arose from the Spanish Civil War of 1936–1939 as a compromise between Falangism and clerical authoritarianism, and whether Franco’s dictatorship was fascist is debated. After a rising in February 1934 Austria had a regime called “Austrofascist”. In Romania the Iron Guard came to power with General Ion Antonescu in 1940, the only fascist movement outside Germany and Italy to do so without foreign help, and was repressed the next year. In Robert Paxton’s account, Salazar crushed Portuguese fascism after copying some of its techniques. Latin America was the continent where fascism was most prominent outside Europe. After 1945 neo-fascist movements followed, among them Italy’s Italian Social Movement and the neo-Nazi groups banned in Germany.
sections.power:
The Acerbo Law and an election won through considerable violence and intimidation entrenched the Fascists in Italy. After the Socialist deputy Giacomo Matteotti was kidnapped and murdered by a Fascist, Mussolini declared himself responsible and in January 1925 proclaimed himself dictator; opposition deputies were barred from parliament and censorship introduced. A corporatist system banned strikes and lock-outs, and by 1934 the state holding company IRI held 48.5 percent of Italy’s share capital. In Libya Fascist Italy waged a campaign of mass killings, concentration camps and the forced starvation of thousands, and expelled 100,000 Bedouin Cyrenaicans, half the population of Cyrenaica. It invaded Ethiopia in 1935.

The Nazis dissolved liberal democracy in Germany in 1933, enacted racial laws that persecuted Jews and other groups, interned open homosexuals in concentration camps and mobilized the country for wars of expansion. Germany annexed Austria in 1938, dismantled Czechoslovakia and invaded Poland in 1939, beginning World War II, which Italy joined in 1940. The Axis Powers in Europe led by Nazi Germany took part in the extermination of millions of Jews, Poles, Roma, Sinti and others in the Holocaust. Mussolini was deposed in 1943 and executed by partisans in April 1945, Hitler killed himself two days later, and Nazi leaders were convicted at Nuremberg of war crimes and crimes against humanity.
sections.critiques:
Fascist parties were contested throughout the interwar years by anti-fascist movements of the centre and left, and during World War II resistance arose in every occupied country, from across the ideological spectrum. The most common criticism is that fascism is a tyranny, deliberately and entirely anti-democratic. Federico Finchelstein wrote that it encompassed totalitarianism, state terrorism, imperialism, racism and, in the German case, “the most radical genocide of the last century: the Holocaust”. Critics have called much of Italian fascism a by-product of Mussolini’s unprincipled opportunism, and its shifting positions on Nazism and race ideologically dishonest: in 1938, on adopting antisemitic laws, Mussolini claimed that Italian fascism had always been antisemitic, though Jewish Italians had been senior fascist officials.

Scholars disagree on a definition; Ian Kershaw likened the attempt to nailing jelly to the wall. Stanley G. Payne, Roger Griffin and Roger Eatwell, the “new consensus”, centre it on a myth of national rebirth, but critics find this too static and too broad. Robert Paxton defines it as behaviour obsessed with community decline that pursues “internal cleansing and external expansion”; John Lukacs denies that a generic fascism exists. In 1944 George Orwell observed that as used, the word had become almost entirely meaningless.
sections.legacy:
The defeat of the Axis powers and the revelation of the Holocaust led to an almost universal condemnation of fascism, past and present, and ended it in general as a state ideology. Since 1945 few parties have openly called themselves fascist, and the word is used across the political spectrum as a pejorative, at times even against communist states. Franco’s one-party state outlasted the war, repressing anti-fascist ideologies and democratic institutions, until his death in 1975 and Spain’s transformation into a liberal democracy.

In the account of Jean-Yves Camus and Nicolas Lebourg, neo-fascist ideology emerged in 1942. In Italy the Italian Social Movement became the self-described “post-fascist” National Alliance; in Germany neo-Nazi movements have been formed and banned under constitutional law that forbids Nazism. Since the Great Recession of 2008 fascism has seen an international surge in popularity. In Greece the Golden Dawn, widely considered neo-Nazi, won seats in parliament, and in 2020 its leader Nikolaos Michaloliakos and six others were found guilty of running a criminal organization. In the United States the 2017 Unite the Right rally drew neo-fascists and neo-Nazis, and groups such as the Proud Boys and Patriot Front were founded. Whether Putin’s Russia is fascist is debated: Timothy Snyder says it is, while Payne, Griffin and Marlène Laruelle disagree.

summary: Fascism is a far-right, ultranationalist ideology that arose in Italy during World War I and came to power under Mussolini in 1922 and Hitler in 1933. Its regimes destroyed democracy, persecuted minorities and opponents and waged wars of conquest, and the genocidal ambitions of the Axis powers murdered millions, above all in the Holocaust. Largely disgraced since 1945, it survives in neo-fascist movements.
references: Benito Mussolini and Giovanni Gentile, The Doctrine of Fascism (1932)
Jason Stanley, How Fascism Works: The Politics of Us and Them (2018)
Umberto Eco, “Eternal Fascism: Fourteen Ways of Looking at a Blackshirt” (1995)

End null: the article treats neo-fascist movements after 1945 as fascist and has a section “Contemporary fascism (2008–present)” describing an “international surge in popularity”; it also says the defeat of the Axis “generally ended fascism as a state ideology”. If the editor prefers the end of the fascist states, 1945 is the year.

Start 1915: the article says the term was first used in 1915 by the Fasces of Revolutionary Action (first meeting 24 January 1915); Olivetti formed an interventionist fascio in October 1914, and the Fasces of Combat followed in 1919. Sternhell traces the ideological roots to the 1880s.
Ethiopia: the fascism article says Italy invaded Ethiopia in 1935; used as given (the imperialism article speaks of a “second invasion of Ethiopia in 1936”).
“Hitler killed himself two days later”: the article gives 28 April 1945 for Mussolini’s execution and 30 April for Hitler’s suicide.
Austria: the article says the February 1934 uprising led to the regime called “Austrofascist”; I wrote “after a rising in February 1934”.
The article does not give a figure for the dead of the Holocaust or the war beyond “millions”; I kept “millions”.

Left out for length: the Fascist Manifesto’s full programme, the Charter of Carnaro and Fiume, Nazi abortion and eugenics law, the Nordicism quarrel, the 6 février 1934 riots in France, Gyula Gömbös in Hungary, and the Klan and “red fascism” as pejorative uses.
